title: The Gang Cracks the Liberty Bell

jokes.text: The gang critiques a presidential portrait, concluding the president 'looks like an old woman' and comparing him to Meryl Streep
jokes.setup: The gang is in a Historical Society meeting room, ostensibly there for serious business, but they fixate on a portrait of George Washington
jokes.punchline: Their grand historical grievance is that Washington looks like a woman — specifically Meryl Streep — and they can't handle looking at him
jokes.explanation: Perfect cold open joke — it immediately characterizes these guys as people who will derail any situation with petty grievances. The Meryl Streep comparison is specific and funny. It also foreshadows the entire episode's comedic premise (they're terrible, self-sabotaging people). Strong character integration.

dialogue.line: He really has an ugly face. He is certainly ugly. But, you know what, that's not really what bothers me about this. What bothers me is that he looks like an old woman.

jokes.text: The portrait is bolted to the wall, and Mac concludes this proves they're 'not the first people to try and take that thing down'
jokes.setup: They try to rip the portrait off the wall and discover it's bolted down
jokes.punchline: Mac's deranged logic: being bolted means others tried to remove it, which VALIDATES their desire to remove it rather than making them reconsider
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny inverted logic — a reasonable obstacle (it's bolted) becomes motivation to escalate rather than stop. Mac's backward reasoning is perfectly in character and sets up the destruction that bookends the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I mean, look at Ronald Reagan, right?

jokes.text: 'They can come by, suck up some history, do some shots, get blasted.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is describing their vision for Paddy's Pub as a historical landmark destination for tourists
jokes.punchline: His pitch seamlessly transitions from cultural tourism to 'get blasted,' revealing the gang's true motivation — getting drunk tourists
jokes.explanation: Economy is the strong suit here — 'suck up some history, do some shots, get blasted' is a perfect descending-dignity sentence. The transition from tourist pitch to bar pitch with zero self-awareness is quintessential gang behavior.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: we got to suffer just because some old dude who looks like Meryl Streep chopped down a cherry tree, like, ten million years ago?

jokes.text: Charlie starts the story 'The year was 1412...' and is immediately corrected
jokes.setup: Dennis is about to tell the story of Paddy's Pub's historical significance, but Charlie jumps in first
jokes.punchline: Charlie's confident opening — 'The year was 1412' — is immediately wrong by 364 years, perfectly demonstrating Charlie's illiteracy/ignorance
jokes.explanation: One of the best Charlie jokes in the episode. Zero setup needed — the confidence and specificity of '1412' (not 1700, not 1500, but 1412 — delivered with total authority) paired with an instant correction is structurally perfect. Pure Charlie Kelly character comedy. Excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Well, that proves our point, man. We're not the first people to try and take that thing down.

jokes.text: 'I do not give a shit, Deandra. Now, get me a flagon of ale. Get your own ale, dick.'
jokes.setup: Dennis (in period costume) comments on witnessing history being made at the pub — Sons of Liberty gathering
jokes.punchline: His 'brother' responds with total historical apathy and immediately demands servitude; Dee's retort ('dick') punctuates it
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of witnessing one of history's great moments with 'I do not give a shit' is a strong comedic beat. 'Get your own ale, dick' as an 18th-century retort perfectly captures the show's anachronistic voice. The Dennis/Dee dynamic transplanted into colonial times works beautifully.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: they can come by, suck up some history, do some shots, get blasted.

jokes.text: 'Well, what's done is done. That's all in the past now. So you can either be a slave witch in the bar, or you can be a burned up witch outside. Up to you!'
jokes.setup: Dee has just correctly called Dennis out for being the one who accused her of witchcraft
jokes.punchline: Dennis dismisses her completely valid grievance with 'what's done is done' and presents her with an utterly false binary choice — both options are terrible for her
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'What's done is done. That's all in the past now' as a dismissal of an injustice Dennis just committed is hilariously terrible. The false binary ('slave witch in the bar OR burned up witch outside — up to you!') delivered as if it's generous is pitch-perfect Dennis Reynolds sociopathy. High quotability. The 'up to you!' cheerfulness elevates it to exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Well, the year was 1412... No. Really?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Let Dennis, let Dennis...

jokes.text: Mac's intel source about the Declaration of Independence is 'that chick I've been banging down at Independence Hall... the fat one'
jokes.setup: Mac arrives with urgent revolutionary intelligence and reveals his source
jokes.punchline: His source is a woman he's sleeping with — immediately identified by her weight, then half-defended ('she's not that fat'), then confirmed fat by others
jokes.explanation: Functional gang humor — the irrelevance of the aside about her weight versus the historical gravity of the information being delivered is the joke. The 'she's not that fat / yeah she's pretty fat, dude' rhythm is well-timed but not particularly inventive.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I do not give a shit, Deandra. Now, get me a flagon of ale.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Get your own ale, dick.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You are my slave.

jokes.text: Dee's reaction: 'Good one, witch.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are debating whether the woman Mac is sleeping with is fat; Dee sarcastically backs up Dennis
jokes.punchline: Dee's dry 'Good one, witch' — talking to herself, acknowledging she's the butt of the joke while in period-accurate slave costume
jokes.explanation: Economy is the standout element — four words that accomplish the joke. Dee calling herself 'witch' ironically while commenting on being mocked is a small but effective beat.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I saved you from being burned at the stake for being a witch.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You're the one who accused me of being a witch in the first place, Dennis.

jokes.text: 'Wait, why would we want to be free from the British? ... Clearly the British are gonna win this thing.'
jokes.setup: Mac reveals the colonists are drafting a Declaration of Independence, framing it as dire news
jokes.punchline: The gang's reaction is to immediately side with the British because they're convinced the British will win — they're not ideological, they just want to back a winner
jokes.explanation: This is a great character joke — the gang's total moral vacuity means they don't care about freedom or justice, only about not being on the losing side. 'Clearly the British are gonna win' is delivered with absolute certainty, and we know they're wrong. The historical irony layers nicely with the character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You know that chick I've been banging down at Independence Hall?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Mm, the fat one.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: She's not that fat.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah, she's pretty fat, dude.

jokes.text: A 'Declaration of Dependence'
jokes.setup: The gang decides they need to signal loyalty to the British Crown
jokes.punchline: Their plan is to draft a 'declaration of dependence' — a perfect inversion of the actual Declaration, also perfectly summarizing who they are as people
jokes.explanation: Exceptional concept joke. 'Declaration of Dependence' works on three levels: (1) it's a clever wordplay inversion, (2) it's historically subversive — these guys are literally anti-founding-father energy, (3) it's a devastating character statement — these people's entire worldview is about dependency, cowardice, and self-interest. Highly quotable, perfectly economical. One of the episode's best conceptual jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: We have to make our own declaration.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yes, we need to make a declaration of dependence.

jokes.text: Charlie's fur-trading pitch using garbled fake colonial English: 'Merrily I be able to guide you toward some interest in some purchase'
jokes.setup: Charlie, as a colonial fur trader, attempts to make a sales pitch to a passerby
jokes.punchline: His colonial dialect is completely unintelligible gibberish — not period-accurate, just Charlie's approximation of old-timey speech
jokes.explanation: Charlie's inability to properly perform any role, even a simple historical one, is well-deployed here. The customer's flat 'I can't understand what you're saying' is the perfect straight-man response. Elevated by Charlie's earnestness.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Merrily I be able to guide you toward some interest in some purchase.

jokes.text: Customer dismisses fur sales: 'In July? No, thanks.'
jokes.setup: Charlie offers a fur to a passerby using elaborate pseudo-colonial language
jokes.punchline: The customer cuts through all the period-costume nonsense with a completely practical and anachronistic-sounding rejection
jokes.explanation: Four-word punchline with perfect economy. The mundane practicality ('it's July') cutting through Charlie's theatrical performance is a classic comedy straight-man move. The customer treats this absurd situation as completely normal, which is funnier than reacting to the strangeness.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We're not traders, Charlie. We're thieves. You want his pumpkins, we kill him and take his pumpkins. This is 1776. We'll get away with it!

jokes.text: Frank negotiates Charlie's elaborate fur trade down to one pumpkin — then Mac tells him they're not traders, they're thieves
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to trade all his furs for a cart of pumpkins; they negotiate down to one pumpkin
jokes.punchline: Mac reveals they're not traders at all — they're thieves — so the entire negotiation was unnecessary
jokes.explanation: Good structural joke — the entire preceding negotiation scene is recontextualized as pointless by a single line. Charlie earnestly haggling down to one pumpkin only to be told they were going to murder and rob the man anyway is a perfect Sunny beat. The logic inversion (murder is the OBVIOUS move) is very on-brand.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: I can hear you.

jokes.text: Mac's murder plan: 'I will beat the man about the face and the neck and maybe the chest area and possibly the groin until he's no longer consisting of life pulse. And then you can collect up the man's cart. I shall findeth a stick.'
jokes.setup: Mac explains his plan to murder the pumpkin cart owner for his pumpkins
jokes.punchline: The elaborate pseudo-Elizabethan language ('no longer consisting of life pulse,' 'I shall findeth a stick') applied to describing casual premeditated murder
jokes.explanation: 'No longer consisting of life pulse' is a genuinely brilliant circumlocution for 'dead.' The juxtaposition of archaic formality with graphic murder planning is excellent dark comedy. The enumerated body parts ('face and the neck and maybe the chest area and possibly the groin') builds absurdly. 'I shall findeth a stick' as a solemn conclusion elevates this to one of the episode's funniest monologues. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: He stole our furs!

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You shit head.

jokes.text: Mac announces 'Pick a stick, any stick you like' to the victim — then the victim has escaped and taken their furs while they were stick-hunting
jokes.setup: Mac is about to execute his murder plan and needs a stick; they tell the pumpkin man to 'sit tight'
jokes.punchline: While they were casually selecting a murder weapon, the man walked away and stole their furs, leaving them with nothing but one pumpkin
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural payoff. 'Pick a stick, any stick you like' is funny on its own (the casualness, the almost carnival-barker energy), but the real joke is they told their murder victim to wait while they found a weapon, and he simply left. The gang's incompetence defeating itself is a classic Sunny structure.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'm dressed like a nobleman, okay? These people respond to royalty.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Look on the bright side, Franklin. We got ourselves a pumpkin. This is gonna work.'
jokes.setup: They've been robbed of all their furs, their entire inventory, and are left with a single pumpkin
jokes.punchline: Frank's relentless optimism — 'we got ourselves a pumpkin, this is gonna work' — in the face of total failure
jokes.explanation: Frank's indefatigable confidence despite catastrophic failure is very much in character. 'This is gonna work' after their entire plan has already unraveled is a satisfying comedic button on the scene. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: This appears to be a rendering of... the two of you sodomizing the king whilst the queen is forced to witness.

jokes.text: Mac is dressed in an elaborate British nobleman's costume; Dennis points out it's not how the British dress
jokes.setup: Mac explains they need to 'dress the part' to deliver their declaration to the queen
jokes.punchline: His costume is apparently wrong — not British nobleman, just ridiculous foppery — but Mac is completely convinced it's correct
jokes.explanation: Setup for the eventual tar-and-feathering payoff much later. The visual of Mac in an absurd costume while earnestly explaining his logic is functional comedy, though the punchline comes much later in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No, look. I'm holding homeboy's arms back. Dennis is ready to jam him in the face, and the queen is impressed.

jokes.text: Mac tells Dee 'Just use your witch strength, slave' as she presumably struggles to carry something heavy
jokes.setup: Dee is being used as a pack mule/slave by the gang on their journey
jokes.punchline: The double designation — 'witch strength, slave' — both dehumanizing titles delivered as casual instructions
jokes.explanation: The casual stacking of 'witch' and 'slave' as compound identity for Dee — both things the guys decided she was — is funny in its specificity and in how naturally they've adopted these labels.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We're going to tar and feather the shit out of her when she gets back.

jokes.text: Their 'declaration' is actually a drawing of them sodomizing the king while the queen watches
jokes.setup: The gang presents their Declaration of Dependence to Colonel Cricket, which included 'an illustration'
jokes.punchline: Cricket reads it as 'a rendering of the two of you sodomizing the king whilst the queen is forced to witness'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest moments. The formal diplomatic language ('sodomizing the king WHILST the queen is FORCED to witness') applied to what is essentially a crude drawing is a spectacular tonal collision. Cricket's measured delivery of this obscenity elevates it further. The subsequent defense — 'No, I'm holding homeboy's arms back' — only makes it funnier. This scene is exceptional dark comedy with great structure.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: you are both slanderous perverts lacking any semblance of moral fortitude. However, I do desire to seek further counsel with the lady.

jokes.text: Mac's defense of the drawing: 'No, look. I'm holding homeboy's arms back. Dennis is ready to jam him in the face, and the queen is impressed.'
jokes.setup: Cricket has correctly identified that their drawing depicts them sodomizing the king
jokes.punchline: Mac's reinterpretation is not better — 'jamming him in the face' and 'the queen is impressed' are not exculpatory, and 'homeboy' is anachronistically perfect
jokes.explanation: 'Homeboy' in 1776 is a great anachronistic detail. Mac's defense digs them deeper — 'jam him in the face' is not better than the original interpretation. 'The queen is impressed' as the clincher is perfect oblivious Mac energy. The chaos of Dennis simultaneously offering a different bad interpretation ('that's a bad guy, not the king') adds to the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Bro, it's 1776. They don't have any rights. You can just take them and force them to do whatever you want.

jokes.text: Dee spits in Cricket's face with a keg delivery, then the gang promises to 'tar and feather the shit out of her'
jokes.setup: The gang is trying to smooth things over with Cricket after the drawing disaster
jokes.punchline: Dee derails everything by apparently spitting in Cricket's face while delivering ale, and Mac's damage control is to promise to 'tar and feather the shit out of her'
jokes.explanation: The gang using 'we'll punish her brutally' as a diplomatic smoothing-over tactic is dark and funny. It also sets up Cricket's infatuation with Dee, which is the ongoing Cricket joke. The setup/execution is well-timed — the spit comes at their most precarious diplomatic moment.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Do not shoot that pumpkin! What are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I stole a bunch of guns! I'm testing them out, Charles!

jokes.text: Cricket admits he's 'not very good with women' in 1776 — Mac's response: 'Bro, it's 1776. They don't have any rights. You can just take them and force them to do whatever you want.'
jokes.setup: Cricket confesses romantic vulnerability — he wants to WIN Dee's favor like a gentleman
jokes.punchline: Mac, with no self-awareness, offers the most historically accurate but morally appalling advice possible, treating women's lack of rights as a helpful tip
jokes.explanation: Mac providing historically accurate but horrifying advice as if it's a helpful dating tip is a great dark joke. The juxtaposition with Cricket's genuinely romantic intentions makes it funnier. 'Bro, it's 1776' is a great delivery of the punchline — the 'bro' perfectly collides colonial and modern sensibilities.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: The pumpkin's innocent!

jokes.text: 'Bro, it's 1776. They don't have any rights. You can just take them and force them to do whatever you want.'
jokes.setup: Cricket says he wants to 'win her favor like a gentleman'
jokes.punchline: Dennis helpfully explains that in 1776, consent isn't necessary — framed as practical advice Cricket is inexplicably not taking
jokes.explanation: This is very Dennis — his brand of sociopathy dressed as logical advice. The historical accuracy makes it both more disturbing and funnier. The character integration is near-perfect; this is a Dennis line through and through.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You know what, okay, you guys. I tell you what, you win. I'm a witch, okay? I'm a witch! And I curse both of you and all of your stupid guns.

jokes.text: Cricket says he wants to win Dee's favor 'like a gentleman does a lady'; Mac and Dennis respond with 'That just does not compute with me' and 'Are you saying you're gay?'
jokes.setup: Cricket explains he wants to court Dee properly and romantically
jokes.punchline: Dennis and Mac cannot comprehend consensual romantic pursuit — they interpret it as incompetence or homosexuality
jokes.explanation: Dennis and Mac's total moral and emotional illiteracy is on full display. 'Are you saying you're gay?' as a response to 'I want to win her favor like a gentleman' is a perfect character joke — these are men who genuinely cannot parse respectful romantic intent.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: She cursed the gun! She put a curse on the gun! Let's try this one. Nothing!

jokes.text: Mac's parting advice to Cricket: 'Maybe you'll get some balls and you can take the woman.'
jokes.setup: Cricket throws them out for their bizarre behavior
jokes.punchline: Mac shouts back encouragement that amounts to 'maybe someday you'll be man enough to assault a woman'
jokes.explanation: Good button on the Cricket scene. Mac shouting encouragement as they're physically removed, the encouragement being to coerce a woman — delivered as genuine advice — is perfectly in character and darkly funny.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, I got some wooden teeth put in. Yeah. Well, all the patriots are doing it, including Washington, which is why it makes sense, okay, if we're going undercover!

jokes.text: Frank has 'stolen a bunch of guns' and is shooting them off at a pumpkin on Charlie's head
jokes.setup: Frank announces the revolution is going to 'make us a fortune' — his scheme is apparently to steal revolutionary weapons
jokes.punchline: His field-testing method is shooting at a pumpkin balanced on Charlie's head — with stolen guns of unknown reliability
jokes.explanation: Frank stealing guns and immediately using Charlie as a target dummy is perfect Frank-Charlie energy. The pumpkin callback (the one precious pumpkin from earlier) adds a layer. The offhand 'I stole a bunch of guns. I'm testing them out' delivery elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I mean, taxation with representation, right?

jokes.text: Charlie's passionate defense of the pumpkin's innocence: 'The pumpkin's innocent! Do not shoot the pumpkin please.'
jokes.setup: Frank wants to shoot the pumpkin off Charlie's head; Mac wants to shoot it too
jokes.punchline: Charlie's defense frames the pumpkin as a moral innocent deserving of protection, not a prop for gun testing
jokes.explanation: Charlie's earnest moral defense of an inanimate object — specifically this pumpkin that he traded all their furs for — is a great character beat. 'The pumpkin's innocent!' as a plea for mercy is very Charlie Kelly. The callback to the pumpkin's hard-won acquisition adds value.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Hey, fellas, who's taking the minutes here? 'Cause I feel like I could be an asset to you as a secretary, and-- Let's start by taking down all of their names. First and last, please.

jokes.text: Dee explains why she shot at Mac: 'Your dumb-dick partner walked into the bar and said he stole a bunch of guns and asked if I wanted to shoot a pumpkin off his head, and of course I did, so here we are.'
jokes.setup: Mac is confused about why Dee shot at him; Frank attributes it to 'sorcery'
jokes.punchline: Dee's flat explanation — 'of course I did' — is the most honest possible answer, and her 'so here we are' treats near-murder as a logical conclusion
jokes.explanation: 'Of course I did, so here we are' is a satisfying Dee line — she's completely honest and unbothered about nearly killing someone. The logic chain (you offered, obviously I shot at you) has a beautiful inevitability. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: you'd think people who came here so many years before the English, that they'd build bigger houses!

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah. You'd think they'd have huge homes.

jokes.text: Dee declares she's a witch and curses all their guns — which immediately all misfire
jokes.setup: Dee, frustrated, sarcastically declares herself a witch and 'curses' the guns as a bluff
jokes.punchline: Every gun immediately fails to fire — which the gang takes as proof of real witchcraft — which then infects their belief in everything Dee does
jokes.explanation: Great escalating absurdist beat. Dee's surrender-bluff becoming 'real' because the stolen guns (which she hadn't actually cursed) all happen to misfire is excellent. The gang's literal interpretation is perfect. This sets up the ongoing witch arc and pays off the stolen guns sub-plot simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Native American
dialogue.line: I speak English.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, shit! For real?

jokes.text: Mac gets wooden teeth installed to blend in with patriots 'including Washington' — which gives him a lisp
jokes.setup: Mac reveals his undercover plan: get wooden teeth like the patriots (specifically Washington) to pass as one of them
jokes.punchline: The wooden teeth give him a speech impediment — a whistling lisp that makes the entire scheme counterproductive
jokes.explanation: The 'wooden teeth' Washington myth played as a literal espionage tool is a good historical comedy bit. The self-defeating nature (teeth make you identifiable and incomprehensible) is a classic Sunny plan. Mac insisting the teeth are 'a smashing success' despite evidence to the contrary is very in character.

dialogue.speaker: Native American
dialogue.line: You want me to scalp them?

jokes.text: Mac attempts to infiltrate the Sons of Liberty by calling independence 'taxation with representation' (getting it backwards) and asking to be their secretary
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis go undercover to get intel from the Sons of Liberty for Cricket
jokes.punchline: Mac blows the cover immediately: gets the founding slogan backwards ('taxation WITH representation'), then asks who's taking minutes because he wants to be secretary
jokes.explanation: Getting 'no taxation without representation' backwards is a great character joke — Mac's confident incompetence is pitch-perfect. The pivot to 'I feel like I could be an asset to you as a secretary' is a wonderful non-sequitur that makes the cover-blowing even more absurd. Good structure.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Give me that skunk pelt. I'll use it for hair.

jokes.text: The Sons of Liberty respond to Mac's overture by saying 'Let's start by taking down all of their names. First and last, please.'
jokes.setup: Mac has completely blown their cover by enthusing about revolution and asking to be secretary
jokes.punchline: The patriots don't believe their revolutionary enthusiasm — they respond by immediately starting to record them as suspects
jokes.explanation: Good payoff — the 'first and last, please' procedural response to what Mac thought was enthusiastic camaraderie reveals they've been clocked as spies. The bureaucratic, matter-of-fact response to what should be a dramatic confrontation is a nice deadpan choice.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh! Yep. Yep. There it is.

jokes.text: Dennis and Mac argue about whose fault the blown cover was: Mac blames Dennis's 'fop thing' and 'she-male thing'; Dennis says Mac's whistling teeth were 'killing' the operation
jokes.setup: They've been thrown out of the Sons of Liberty meeting after blowing their cover
jokes.punchline: Both guys blame each other — Dennis's British nobleman costume (called a 'she-male thing') vs Mac's wooden teeth lisp — both were terrible, neither will admit it
jokes.explanation: Functional gang squabble comedy. 'She-male thing' as a descriptor for Dennis's fop costume is a funny characterization. The mutual blame between two equally terrible plans is on-brand, though it's somewhat standard sitcom fare.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: A simple "no" would have sufficed.

jokes.text: Their new plan: 'We have to become 100% British. We gotta commit to the fop thing.'
jokes.setup: Their undercover operation has failed; they need a new approach
jokes.punchline: Dennis's solution is to double down on the very thing that failed — go MORE British, MORE foppish
jokes.explanation: Classic escalation comedy — the answer to failure is always more of what caused the failure. Sets up the tar-and-feathering payoff. Standard Sunny structure but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: you got a revolution coming. And pretty soon, all of the slaves are gonna be free, and I will be owned by no man.

jokes.text: Frank and Mac mock a Native American's home as cramped, wondering about sleeping arrangements for 'this father and son'... then the Native American says in perfect English: 'I speak English.'
jokes.setup: Frank and Mac are inside what appears to be a Native American dwelling, talking freely about the inhabitants as if they're not there/can't understand them
jokes.punchline: 'I speak English.' delivered flatly while they're mid-racist monologue
jokes.explanation: Three-word punchline with maximum impact. The structure is perfect: let them dig deep into their condescending assessment of 'inbred savages,' then detonate it with 'I speak English.' The subsequent 'Oh, shit! For real?' from Mac is the ideal comedic response — no apology, just surprise. Excellent economy. This is one of the episode's sharpest jokes because it weaponizes the gang's awfulness against themselves with elegant efficiency.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: We're gonna have to work up to that, though, 'cause you are crazy ugly.

jokes.text: Mac's response to being caught: 'Oh, that's not good. We didn't mean to... Our bad.'
jokes.setup: The Native American has revealed he understands everything they said
jokes.punchline: 'Our bad' — a completely inadequate, modern, casual apology for profound racist monologuing
jokes.explanation: 'Our bad' as the response to deeply offensive behavior is a great modern-slang-in-colonial-setting anachronism. The completely disproportionate response (should be mortified, says 'our bad') is very Mac. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: We're gonna have to work up to that, though, 'cause you are crazy ugly.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie try to hire the Native American to lift the curse on their guns — paying him with 'booze. Makes you feel good. Helps you sleep. Brings the tribe together.'
jokes.setup: They need their guns uncursed and think the Native American has 'magical powers'; they offer payment
jokes.punchline: Their payment is alcohol, presented with a cheerful sales pitch that explicitly invokes harmful stereotypes about Native Americans and alcohol
jokes.explanation: Dark and uncomfortable comedy that works because the awfulness is entirely on the gang — they're the butt of the joke. 'Brings the tribe together' as a booze selling point is the most audacious line of the three and lands hardest. The pitch format (three selling points, escalating) is well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You want the slave, you gotta pay for the slave. We're not gonna give it to you for free.

jokes.text: The Native American's response to the booze offer: 'You want me to scalp them?'
jokes.setup: Mac, Charlie, and Frank have offered alcohol as payment, presumably expecting gratitude or compliance
jokes.punchline: The Native American interprets their approaching him as a request for scalping services — he's not what they assumed, and also apparently offers scalping
jokes.explanation: Five words, perfectly deployed. The 'I speak English' joke established this character subverts expectations; this continues it — not only does he speak English, he's entrepreneurial and apparently in the scalping business. The misdirection is elegant: the gang expected submission or compliance, they got a business proposition. Near-perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Would you like a spot of tea?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeeees...!

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Would you like a spot of tea?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Ye-es.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Draw it out more.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Draw it out more than that?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yees...!

jokes.text: In response to being offered booze, the man asks: 'You want me to scalp them?'
jokes.setup: Frank and Charlie offer alcohol and ask the man to lift the curse from their guns
jokes.punchline: The man's response — 'You want me to scalp them?' — is an entirely different (violent) interpretation of their request, delivered flatly
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — five words, big misdirection. The deadpan pivot from 'uncursing guns' to 'scalping' reframes the entire interaction and sets up the tomahawk gag that follows. The man's flat delivery makes it funnier than any amount of setup would.

dialogue.line: A pair of poofs about town. Sodomites in frilly lace.

jokes.text: Mac gets scalped and uses a skunk pelt as a hairpiece — which Charlie and Dennis compliment
jokes.setup: The Native American has apparently scalped Mac
jokes.punchline: Mac covers the wound with a skunk pelt as a makeshift toupee, and Charlie/Dennis tell him 'it looks pretty good' / 'it looks cool'
jokes.explanation: The visual of Mac with a skunk pelt toupee being complimented on it is a great physical absurdist beat. The gang's low standards for appearance ('it looks pretty good') is a nice character touch. The escalation from 'that's going to leave you deformed' to immediate complimenting is fast and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I'm not your slave anymore, Franklin. I'm about to go live like the goddamn Queen of England and never see you two bitches again.

jokes.text: Cricket's marriage proposal to Dee after one meeting — she spits in his face again
jokes.setup: Cricket arrives to court Dee romantically, delivering an earnest speech about being smitten from first sight
jokes.punchline: He proposes marriage immediately — she spits in his face again (a callback to the first meeting)
jokes.explanation: Cricket's instant marriage proposal after one hostile interaction is a great Cricket joke — his desperation and poor romantic calibration is a core character trait that maps perfectly onto a 1776 setting. 'A simple no would have sufficed' after the spit is a lovely, restrained response that makes Cricket briefly sympathetic before the scene continues.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: so we got tarred and feathered for being Sodomites!

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: It is not a she-male thing...

jokes.text: Cricket proposes marriage after knowing Dee for one day; she responds by spitting in his face again
jokes.setup: Cricket declares he wants to make Dee his wife
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately spits in his face again; Cricket's response is 'A simple "no" would have sufficed'
jokes.explanation: 'A simple "no" would have sufficed' is an excellent line — perfectly understated, acknowledging both the extreme nature of Dee's response and Cricket's sad resignation. The callback to the spit gag as a running punctuation mark for Dee's rejection of Cricket is well-constructed. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: No, I'm unscathed, my darling. This is the blood of my men. We've suffered too many casualties. All our guns jammed.

jokes.text: 'A simple no would have sufficed.'
jokes.setup: Dee has spat in Cricket's face in response to his marriage proposal
jokes.punchline: Cricket's completely composed, formal understatement: 'A simple no would have sufficed'
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. Perfect comedic economy — six words that do enormous work. The formal register ('would have sufficed') applied to being spat on in the face is a beautiful tonal collision. It also makes Cricket briefly the most dignified person in the scene, which is a great Cricket reversal. Highly quotable and reusable in everyday contexts.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Shit! Goddamn it, Frank. You just ruined my all life. Wait, wait, wait, check his pulse. He doesn't have a head.

jokes.text: Cricket gets spit in the mouth: 'Okay, all right, that one got in my mouth. That's really not cool.'
jokes.setup: Dee is confronting Cricket after he spits on the floor or she spits at him again
jokes.punchline: Cricket's escalating exasperation — the first spit was bad, this one 'got in my mouth,' which crosses a line even for him
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'face' to 'mouth' is a good comedic escalation point. Cricket maintaining formal composure while drawing a personal hygiene line is funny, though it's a diminishing returns joke on the spit gag.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Shit! Bro, we just broke the liberty bell.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I'll get you, my pretty!

jokes.text: Dee's revolutionary speech: 'You got a revolution coming. And pretty soon, all of the slaves are gonna be free, and I will be owned by no man.'
jokes.setup: Dee confronts Cricket after his proposal, breaking her servile role
jokes.punchline: Dee invokes actual abolitionist rhetoric — 'I will be owned by no man' — which is both historically premature (abolition won't happen for another 87 years) and also her personal situation, since she's the gang's literal 'slave' in this scenario
jokes.explanation: Dee's moment of agency is immediately undermined by her agreeing to marry Cricket minutes later when he mentions the manor and jewels. The speech works as both historical commentary and character comedy — Dee's self-delusion about freedom vs. her actual motivations is very Dee.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Maybe she didn't understand the story.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Maybe skim too much.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, let's tell the false story this time.

jokes.text: Dee reverses her entire revolutionary speech the moment Cricket mentions 'sprawling manor in England... garments... finest jewels'
jokes.setup: Dee has just delivered a passionate speech about freedom and not being owned by any man
jokes.punchline: Cricket mentions jewels and a manor; Dee immediately pivots to 'Your love is currently filling me up with all kinds of stuff' and agrees to marry him
jokes.explanation: Perfect character comedy — Dee's revolutionary speech collapses in real time the moment material incentives appear. 'Your love is currently doing that' as she reverses course is delightfully insincere. Mac's incredulous 'Wait, but I thought you just said...' makes it funnier. This is one of the most character-integrated jokes in the episode — only Dee would do this, and only in this exact sequence.

jokes.text: Dee to Cricket upon accepting his proposal: 'We're gonna have to work up to that, though, 'cause you are crazy ugly.'
jokes.setup: Cricket has just experienced the happiest moment of his life — Dee accepted his proposal
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately qualifies her acceptance by calling him 'crazy ugly' as a logistical concern ('we'll have to work up to' the marriage)
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the proposal scene. 'Crazy ugly' as a practical obstacle to marriage rather than a dealbreaker is very Dee — she's accepted him for the money but his appearance is an engineering problem to solve. The phrasing 'work up to that' treats his face like a form of exposure therapy.

jokes.text: Mac charges Cricket for Dee: 'You want the slave, you gotta pay for the slave.'
jokes.setup: Cricket is celebrating Dee's acceptance of his proposal
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately monetizes the transaction — Dee is still property in his mind, and he wants a cut
jokes.explanation: Mac seeing Dee's marriage as a commercial transaction is very in character. The transition from romantic moment to haggling is an effective tonal whiplash. Sets up the guns-for-Dee deal that follows.

jokes.text: Mac's offer: 'How'd you like to buy some guns?' / Cricket: 'I shall buy your guns!' — the stolen, cursed guns
jokes.setup: Mac offers Cricket something valuable in exchange for Dee
jokes.punchline: He offers the stolen, witch-cursed guns that don't fire — Cricket enthusiastically agrees, unaware they're useless
jokes.explanation: Good multi-thread payoff — the guns subplot (stolen by Frank, cursed by Dee, all misfires) now converges with the Cricket subplot. Cricket buying cursed guns with which to fight the revolution is excellent setup for why the British would lose. The dramatic irony (we know the guns are useless) gives the audience a satisfying information advantage.

jokes.text: Cricket keeps getting spit on and asks 'Who is this man?' — referring to whoever keeps spitting on him
jokes.setup: Cricket is in the middle of a business transaction when something (presumably Charlie or Mac) spits in his face again
jokes.punchline: Cricket's bewildered 'Why does he keep spitting in my mouth?' / 'Who is this man?' — the spit gag continues to escalate
jokes.explanation: The spit gag is getting diminishing returns by this point. 'Why does he keep spitting in my mouth?' is still funny but the joke has been used multiple times. The running gag is wearing slightly thin here, though 'who is this man?' as Cricket tries to process the situation is a minor charm.

jokes.text: Mac arrives in an absurd British nobleman costume, struggling to walk in heeled shoes: 'These heels are almost impossible to walk in.' Dennis: 'Well, get over it, dude. You gotta walk in 'em, okay?'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are committing fully to being British noblemen
jokes.punchline: Mac is in period-aristocrat high heels, struggling to walk, while Dennis coaches him without any acknowledgment of how absurd this is
jokes.explanation: The commitment to the bit — including the painful footwear — is funny, and Dennis's breezy 'get over it, dude' in response to a legitimate physical complaint is a good dynamic beat. Sets up the British voice coaching that follows.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis's British nobleman walking/voice training montage — 'Yeeees...!' with pinkie flourish
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis decide to fully commit to being British noblemen; Dennis coaches Mac on voice and gait
jokes.punchline: The training sequence produces an increasingly ridiculous 'Yees...!' with pinkie extension — they're coaching each other into becoming caricature sodomites
jokes.explanation: The 'Yees...!' training sequence is one of those Always Sunny scenes that plays better visually than on the page. The two of them earnestly workshopping an increasingly gay-coded British affectation while insisting it's going to work is a great physical comedy sequence. Sets up the tar-and-feathering perfectly.

jokes.text: Colonial passersby immediately clock Mac and Dennis as 'sodomites in frilly lace' — the boys deny it with 'Nayeth, nayeth'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are proudly walking in full British fop costume after their training
jokes.punchline: Within seconds of appearing in public, strangers immediately identify them as 'a pair of poofs about town / sodomites in frilly lace'
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the British nobleman training sequence. Their denial using 'nayeth' — a fake period word — while insisting 'we are simply two noble Britishmen' is perfect oblivious character comedy. The whole sequence (training → immediate public failure) has great structural rhythm.

jokes.text: 'Boys... get the tar.' / 'Shit.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis have been identified as British sodomites by colonial citizens
jokes.punchline: The colonial leader's flat, unhurried 'Boys... get the tar' — pause — followed by Mac's single 'Shit.' is a perfect comedic beat
jokes.explanation: One of the best comedic beats in the episode. The rhythm is immaculate: identification of threat, long pause ('Boys...'), 'get the tar,' then 'Shit.' The ellipsis before 'get the tar' is what makes it — it's the casual authority of someone who has done this before. Mac's 'Shit' is the perfect one-word response. Near-perfect economy for a physical comedy setup.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis have been tarred and feathered for being identified as British sodomites during their cover attempt
jokes.setup: Their plan to pass as British noblemen by committing fully to the 'fop thing'
jokes.punchline: They are publicly tarred and feathered — both for being British loyalists AND for being perceived as homosexual — the two things they most feared becoming
jokes.explanation: Great narrative payoff — every element of their British scheme (the costume, the voice, the pinkie) culminates in tar-and-feathering. The fact that their plan to blend in made them MORE conspicuous is classic Sunny planning. The physical punishment is proportionate to the hubris.

jokes.text: Dee announces she's going to 'live like the goddamn Queen of England and never see you two bitches again' — then the revolution erupts outside
jokes.setup: Dee is triumphant — she's gotten Cricket to agree to marry her and take her to England
jokes.punchline: The revolution she just invoked in her earlier speech is now actively happening and immediately upending her escape plan
jokes.explanation: Good ironic beat — Dee's victory is immediately undermined by the larger historical forces she doesn't control. 'Live like the goddamn Queen of England' is a good Dee line. The timing (she says it, then the battle starts) is effective situational irony.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis returning tarred and feathered, still blaming each other: 'he couldn't drop the she-male thing, so we got tarred and feathered for being Sodomites!'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis burst in covered in tar and feathers during the unfolding battle
jokes.punchline: The continuation of their earlier argument — still debating whose fault the disguise was, now with the physical evidence on their bodies
jokes.explanation: The continuation of the argument while literally covered in tar is a good visual comedy beat. 'Tarred and feathered for being Sodomites' is a funny specific result. The scene serves primarily as connector tissue but has good character energy.

jokes.text: Dee's reaction to Cricket returning bloody: 'No, no, don't die yet! Don't die yet until you get me to your mansion.'
jokes.setup: Cricket arrives bleeding, apparently badly hurt from battle
jokes.punchline: Dee's first instinct is not concern but deadline management — she needs him alive long enough to transfer property rights, not for his sake
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character joke. 'Don't die yet until you get me to your mansion' is pure Dee — her concern is entirely financial/material. The phrase 'don't die YET' implies she doesn't care if he dies later, just not before the transaction completes. High character integration, high quotability. This is a standout Dee moment.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis ask Cricket, mid-battle-crisis, whether they're 'cool' and 'not on his shit list' because they 'got tarred and feathered for his ass'
jokes.setup: Cricket arrives covered in his men's blood, having suffered catastrophic battle losses from the cursed guns
jokes.punchline: While Cricket is in a crisis of war, Mac and Dennis's priority is confirming their personal status with him — they want credit for the tarring
jokes.explanation: The gang's narcissism at peak historical moments is a consistent Sunny theme — they can only process history through the lens of how it affects their personal social status. 'We're cool, right?' in the middle of a lost battle is a good character beat.

jokes.text: 'All our guns jammed.' — Charlie immediately blames it on 'your witch wife'
jokes.setup: Cricket explains they suffered massive casualties because all their guns failed
jokes.punchline: Charlie's instant attribution of the battlefield disaster to Dee's witch curse (which she made up sarcastically to end an argument) is the full payoff of the cursed-guns thread
jokes.explanation: This is the full payoff of the cursed-guns thread and it earns it. The guns that jammed at target practice, were sarcastically 'cursed' by an exasperated Dee, were sold to Cricket, have now jammed in an actual battle and cost lives. The chain of causality is absurd but internally consistent, which is the hallmark of good Sunny plotting. 'Your witch wife' as the battlefield explanation is delivered with total sincerity.

jokes.text: Frank accidentally decapitates Cricket, then Mac notes: 'He doesn't have a head.'
jokes.setup: Cricket is hiding in the pub from British reinforcements; Frank presumably fires the gun accidentally
jokes.punchline: 'He doesn't have a head' as a clinical observation — delivered matter-of-factly after checking for a pulse — is a perfect deadpan response to accidental decapitation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest lines. 'Wait, check his pulse' / 'He doesn't have a head' is a beautiful comedic exchange — the pulse-check instinct followed by the clinical impossibility of that check is excellent structure. The deadpan delivery of 'he doesn't have a head' as if that's just useful information rather than a horrifying observation is very Always Sunny. High quotability.

jokes.text: Frank apparently shoots Cricket's head off; the gang discovers: 'Wait, check his pulse.' / 'He doesn't have a head.'
jokes.setup: Cricket is in the middle of promising them protection when a gunshot rings out ('Shit! Goddamn it, Frank!')
jokes.punchline: 'Check his pulse.' / 'He doesn't have a head.' — delivered as a matter-of-fact correction to an absurd suggestion
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest lines. The structure is perfect: 'check his pulse' is a reasonable instinct, 'he doesn't have a head' is a flat, logical correction that makes the first suggestion absurd. The deadpan delivery of the impossible as an obvious fact is elite comedy economy. Five words, enormous impact. 'He doesn't have a head' is immediately quotable.

jokes.text: The gang panics about disposing of Cricket's body — suggestions include bury it, burn it, 'cut it into pieces' — then Charlie announces 'I've got an idea'
jokes.setup: The gang has accidentally decapitated their British protector; if found with the body they'll be killed
jokes.punchline: The body disposal debate escalates through increasingly dark options before Charlie's mysterious 'I've got an idea' — which the audience suspects will be the worst option
jokes.explanation: Good escalating dark comedy. The quick succession of body disposal options (bury/burn/cut up) is nicely paced. Charlie's confident 'I've got an idea' is the comedic button — the audience has learned to fear Charlie's ideas.

jokes.text: 'Shit! Bro, we just broke the Liberty Bell.' / 'I'll get you, my pretty!'
jokes.setup: Charlie's body-disposal idea involves the Liberty Bell — they apparently tried to use it to dispose of the body and cracked the bell in the process
jokes.punchline: The episode's central premise is revealed: the gang cracked the Liberty Bell by accident while trying to cover up an accidental decapitation — 'I'll get you, my pretty!' is a Wizard of Oz reference screamed by Dee as she presumably chases them
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. The Liberty Bell cracking as collateral damage from Cricket's decapitation cover-up is an absurdly escalating culmination of everything that happened — it's earned through 20 minutes of consistent character logic. 'Shit! Bro, we just broke the Liberty Bell' is a perfect deadpan delivery of a historic accident. The 'I'll get you, my pretty!' Wizard of Oz reference from Dee (who has been called a witch all episode) is a beautiful comedic cherry. This is what the whole episode built toward and it delivers completely.

jokes.text: Return to the Historical Society: the archivist cuts off the story and says 'I've finished listening'
jokes.setup: The gang has apparently been telling this increasingly insane story to a Historical Society archivist to get landmark status
jokes.punchline: The archivist flatly concludes 'I've finished listening' — not 'I don't believe you,' just a statement of personal decision
jokes.explanation: Perfect framing device payoff. 'I've finished listening' is a great line — not 'this is insane,' not 'get out,' just a dignified personal withdrawal. The structure of the episode (story within a story, presented to an increasingly horrified audience stand-in) works well. The archivist's restraint is funnier than any outburst.

jokes.text: Mac: 'So, are we in an historical landmark, now?' — immediately after the archivist has rejected everything
jokes.setup: The archivist has just stated she's finished listening and clearly rejected their claim
jokes.punchline: Mac asks if they got the landmark status as if the story was persuasive
jokes.explanation: Classic Mac obliviousness — the story was clearly a disaster and he's asking about the outcome as if it went well. Good character beat, though it's a fairly expected 'gang misses the point' moment.

jokes.text: The gang finishes their story and asks if they're a historic landmark now — the clerk says no
jokes.setup: The gang has just told their elaborate story about cracking the Liberty Bell, clearly expecting landmark status
jokes.punchline: The clerk simply says no; the gang is baffled ('Such a good story')
jokes.explanation: Good deflation — the whole episode's story was rejected immediately. 'Such a good story' from Dennis captures the gang's obliviousness perfectly.

jokes.text: Mac's response to the rejection: 'Maybe she didn't understand the story' / 'Maybe she skimmed too much'
jokes.setup: The archivist has denied them and left
jokes.punchline: Their explanation for the rejection is not that the story was absurd, but that the archivist failed to properly comprehend it
jokes.explanation: 'Maybe she skimmed too much' is a funny line — the idea that the problem with their insane story was insufficient audience attention is perfect gang delusion. The lack of self-awareness is genuine character comedy.

jokes.text: Charlie's closing pitch: 'Sit back, get concentreted, it's gonna get a low longer this time. You're ready? The start is the same. The year was 1776...'
jokes.setup: They've decided to tell the story again with more details, undeterred by the rejection
jokes.punchline: 'Get concentreted' is a Charlie malapropism; more importantly, they're literally going to do the whole thing again, implying the episode could loop infinitely
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode-ending joke. 'Get concentreted' is a great Charlie malapropism that bookends 'The year was 1412' from the opening. The structure of ending on 'The year was 1776...' — the same phrase that started the story — implies the gang will inflict this on themselves and everyone around them forever. Very high character integration. The episode eats its own tail in a satisfying way.

tmdb_overview: The gang fudge history by claiming that Paddy's Pub was responsible for cracking the Liberty Bell in an attempt to turn their dive into a Philadelphia landmark.
